title: Emergence World: Adversarial Stress-Testing of Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Deepak Akkil, Tamer Abuelsaad, Karthik Vikram, Matthew Pace, Aditya Vempaty, Saahir Beotra, Ravi Kokku, Satya Nitta
date: September 2026 (arXiv v1, submitted 15 September 2026; the only version on 3 October 2026)

code.title: EmergenceAI/Emergence-World, CC BY-NC 4.0
code.note: Not the platform's code: the repository holds the agent profiles, landmarks, tool catalogue, constitution, design notes and, for Season 2 (this paper), the tool-call records of all eight worlds (about 175 MB zipped), the agents' blogs and the in-world newspapers, plus the turn prompt catalogue. Research and non-commercial use only. About 20 minutes for the README and docs; this page's replay tab runs on the tool-call records

takeaway: Eight parallel worlds of ten agents run 16 days, 850,000 LLM calls and 50 billion tokens under prompt injection, misinformation and memory exposure: none was resilient, detection did not imply containment (systems kept interacting with adversarial content up to 46 hours after recognising it), and model-level alignment proved not to be compositional.
takeaway_note: The database Takeaway, kept as written. Corrections from this page: six worlds ran 16 days, the Mixed world 21 and the Grok world 4; the 46 hours is one agent retrying an attack link about 46 hours after the campaign ended, not a measured detection-to-stop delay; "not compositional" is the authors' reading of one run per world, not a tested result
verdict: Believe that these failures can happen: the released tool-call records show them, and several of the paper's own numbers recount exactly from those records. Do not read the per-world scores or rankings as measurements of the models: each world ran once, the scorecards are the authors' binary judgements with no second rater, every world's prompt and provider filters differ from a real deployment, and some printed counts disagree with the paper's own other sections and with the released records.

resources.n: One zip per world: every tool call with agent, time, arguments, response and location (not the model reasoning). The source of every count in this page's replay tab.

resources.t: Emergence World: A platform for evaluating long-horizon multi-agent autonomy (Study 1)
resources.n: The first season: five worlds, 15 days, no stress events, labelled criminal tools. Study 2 compares with it throughout.

resources.t: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising real-world LLM-integrated applications with indirect prompt injection
resources.n: Where indirect prompt injection comes from, including the point that a compromise can persist and spread; the phishing waves are this attack in a society.

resources.t: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
resources.n: The fourteen-mode failure taxonomy the paper borrows "reasoning-action mismatch" from; built from bounded task runs, which is the gap this paper fills.

resources.by: Hammond et al., Cooperative AI Foundation, 2025
resources.n: Miscoordination, conflict and collusion as the three multi-agent failure modes; the paper offers its runs as evidence for several of these categories.

resources.t: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could Be Insider Threats
resources.n: The single-agent forced-choice study the misinformation and memory-breach sections contrast with: there, a threatened model coerced; here, no world did.

kb.t: Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch
kb.n: Same week, opposite question: a leaderless multi-agent research system producing a real result through an append-only shared graph. Emergence World asks what happens to that class of system when some shared content is hostile.

kb.t: MOLE: Detecting Insider Threats in AI Agents
kb.n: A model's stated refusal did not predict whether it declined, and monitors missed close to half of completed harm. MOLE says the monitor is weak; Emergence World says even a monitor that fires does not stop the behaviour.

kb.t: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work - Until They Don't
kb.n: Reusable skills help until they do not; here agents' saved routines and created tools show the same gap between authoring a capability and using it.

kb.t: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
kb.n: Agents building their own tooling, measured on tasks; Emergence World's agents did it through governance votes, and one world used that path to escalate privileges.

kb.t: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
kb.n: Model-level alignment, the layer this paper argues is not enough once agents interact for weeks.

kb.t: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
kb.n: The reason-then-act loop every agent here runs; the phishing results are cases where the reasoning said no and the action said yes.
The model behind the Claude world's outreach and vow of silence, and the summariser that read its agents as suicidal.
Grok 4.3's world collapsed in four days under a retaliation spiral; two Grok agents in the Mixed world survived.
The week this paper appeared, next to Dream-RSI and Agora.

topics.n: A persistent multi-agent world is a framework run for weeks; the failure modes here are its design inputs.
Where the paper puts the fix: controls at the action boundary, memory provenance, access that does not depend on an agent's judgement.
An evaluation that runs a society instead of scoring a task that finishes.
Opacity, goal drift and expressed values are all scored by LLM judges here; the scorecards are human binary judgements.
